edits.new: The appraisal document of 13 February 2012 prints one legal covenant and no condition of effectiveness or disbursement. The covenant binds the borrower, through the Ministry of Railways, to implement the project and to make the provinces implement it in accordance with the safeguards instruments, in a manner and substance satisfactory to the Bank, and to monitor those instruments every six months. The project was Environmental Category A, and four safeguard policies were triggered: environmental assessment (OP/BP 4.01), natural habitats (OP/BP 4.04), physical cultural resources (OP/BP 4.11) and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). To meet OP 4.12 the ministry had to prepare a resettlement action plan, a resettlement policy framework and a social assessment, all acceptable to the Bank. The plan had to set out how grievances would be handled, how resettlement would be monitored inside and outside the project, and where the money for it would come from, and it had to be published; it was disclosed in China on 4 January 2012. Each county government involved signed a letter committing itself to carry it out. Procurement plans and any change to them had to go to the Bank for prior review and no objection before use.

The appraisal document of 14 April 2010 lists the loan's conditions and covenants and leaves the line for effectiveness conditions blank. The loan had to be passed down in a fixed way: the borrower on-lent it to Anhui province and Anhui to Anqing, Huaibei, Lu'an and Wuhu on the same terms, with the municipalities carrying the currency risk. Anhui and the four cities had to keep an adequate organisational structure in place. Anhui had to make each city carry out its resettlement action plan and environmental management plan, prepare and carry out annual work plans, hire consultants to supervise the works, and hire consultants to monitor how the resettlement and environmental plans were being carried out, send the Bank the results every six months and act on their recommendations. Anhui also owed six-monthly project reports and a mid-term report by 15 August 2013. The project was Environmental Category B and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) was triggered. That monitoring covenant is how the households left in temporary housing came to be counted at all: the external consultant reported under it.

This is the one loan of these ten where resettlement sat in the condition that had to be met before the money could be drawn. The appraisal document of 28 May 2004 sets out a single condition of effectiveness: a legal opinion confirming that the resettlement arrangements between the Ministry of Railways and each of the provinces of Hunan, Jiangxi and Zhejiang, entered into to cause the resettlement action plan to be carried out, were legally binding on the parties. The ministry then had standing obligations: to take all necessary actions to minimise as far as possible any involuntary loss by people of shelter, productive assets, access to productive assets, income or means of livelihood, temporary or permanent; to carry out the environmental management plan, the resettlement plan and those arrangements in a manner satisfactory to the Bank; and to send any proposed change to the three to the Bank for approval. Other covenants were about the railway: power supply agreements by 1 August 2006, a timetable for the new trains by 31 December 2004, operating rules by 1 August 2006, and twice-yearly financial and yearly results reporting. The project was Environmental Category A.

The appraisal document of 20 May 2013 prints one condition of effectiveness and six legal covenants. The condition was that a subsidiary agreement be executed between the project implementing entity, Nanchang Municipality and the Urban Rail Company. The covenants required the implementing entity to keep an organisational structure satisfactory to the Bank, including a Project Leading Group to oversee the work and a Project Management Office to run it; to carry out the Integration Plan as approved; to make the municipality and the rail company carry out the safeguards instruments in a manner and substance satisfactory to the Bank; and to furnish six-monthly project reports, half-yearly interim financial reports and audited financial statements within six months of each year's end. The project was Environmental Category A, and environmental assessment (OP/BP 4.01), physical cultural resources (OP 4.11) and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) were triggered. Under OP 4.12 the project office prepared a resettlement action plan, with a resettlement policy framework for parts of the works that might move, and both were disclosed. The compensation was paid by the client and not out of the loan, but the safeguards covenant applied to it all the same.

The appraisal document of 30 May 2006 sets out two conditions of effectiveness: eight subsidiary loan agreements, satisfactory to the Bank, signed between the project counties and their water utility companies; and financial management training given to all staff responsible for implementation, a condition to be dropped if Henan showed before signing that it was already done. A disbursement covenant made spending under a subproject eligible only where that county's subsidiary loan agreement was signed and a legal opinion confirmed it. Other covenants: Bank review of five competitive bidding contracts before the bid documents were finished; improvement action plans for the low-performing water companies by 31 December 2006; dam remedial works in Baofeng and Queshan counties; and a financial covenant requiring each water company to earn revenues at least equal to its operating expenses plus the excess of debt service over depreciation plus its own capital spending. On the land taking, what the agreement carried was a duty to report rather than a duty to deliver: Schedule 2, paragraph 4(b) required six-monthly monitoring and evaluation reports on the environmental management plan and the resettlement action plan, under terms of reference satisfactory to the Bank. The completion report records that covenant as only partially complied with. Neither the covenant list nor the report's compliance tables prints a term requiring the resettlement plan itself to be carried out.

The appraisal document of 20 January 2012 prints thirteen conditions and legal covenants, all under the project agreement with Sichuan, and no condition of effectiveness. Sichuan had to keep the project's leading groups and project offices in place to 31 December 2017. It had to apply the project implementation plan, the resettlement action plan, the environmental management plan, the pest management plan and the annual dam safety action plan in a manner satisfactory to the Bank, and could not amend, suspend or waive any of them without the Bank's prior agreement. Two covenants went directly to the people moved: Sichuan had to carry out measures satisfactory to the Bank for improving the living standard of displaced persons in accordance with the resettlement plan, and had to hire and keep independent consultants to monitor and report annually from outside the project, then act promptly on their recommendations, in order to improve compliance with that plan. Works contracts had to carry provisions enforcing the environmental plan, with penalties for failure written in. The rest covered a dam safety panel and dam safety plans, six-monthly reporting, a mid-term review by 30 June 2015, and water user associations in each county. Environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, involuntary resettlement and safety of dams were triggered, at Environmental Category A.

The appraisal document of 24 April 2012 prints five legal covenants and no condition of effectiveness or disbursement. Yining Municipality had to keep an adequate organisational structure in place; carry out the environmental management plan, the resettlement action plan and the Ethnic Minority Development Plan; send the Bank six-monthly project reports; send six-monthly progress reports on how those three plans were being carried out; and send a mid-term progress report by 30 June 2015. Environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) were triggered, at Environmental Category B. The resettlement plan was prepared because OP 4.12 requires one. The Ethnic Minority Development Plan came out of the social assessment and was written to make the design meet the needs of local Uygur communities. What the agreement did not carry is a sum of money. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the US$19.5 million the appraisal document says was budgeted for compensation and resettlement appears in no project cost table, and that spending on land acquisition is not mentioned in the appraisal document, the loan agreement or the completion report. The duty to carry out the plan was covenanted; the cost of doing so was never fixed in the loan documents.

This loan is the plainest case of nothing added. The appraisal document of 15 March 2011 has a section headed loan conditions and covenants, and it says in full: effectiveness conditions, "No non-standard conditions"; covenants, standard ones relating to procurement, financial management and safeguards. The data sheet's line for effectiveness conditions reads "None." No term particular to this project was attached to the money. The project was Environmental Category A and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) was triggered, so a resettlement plan with a resettlement policy framework had to be prepared, and was. The completion report describes the standard reporting that went with it: interim financial reports, annual audited reports, periodic reports on safeguards implementation and regular progress reports in agreed formats, with independent consultants commissioned to monitor the social safeguards. None of it covered what happened at Sanba village, because the households were moved off the resettlement site in January 2018, after the loan closed on 31 December 2017. The arrangements that followed, Yingshang County's six-monthly reports on the resettlement housing, the provincial office's continued monitoring and the grievance mechanism, were undertakings given under a later project, the Anhui Rural Road Program, not conditions of this loan.

The appraisal document of 5 May 2010 records no condition of effectiveness: the line reads "Loan Effectiveness: None." There was one condition of disbursement, that subsidiary loan or implementation agreements acceptable to the Bank be signed between the districts and counties and their implementing agencies. Five implementation covenants followed: keep the Chongqing project management office and the local implementation units qualified and staffed; on-lend the loan proceeds on terms satisfactory to the Bank; provide adequate funding for counterpart requirements, debt repayments and maintenance; show the Bank that a clinic met municipal standards before Bank-financed equipment was delivered to it; and hold a mid-term review. Environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement (OP 4.12) and safety of dams were triggered, at Environmental Category B. Six resettlement action plans were prepared under Chinese law and OP 4.12, and a consolidated plan was translated into English for the Bank's review and approval. The covenant list prints nothing requiring those plans to be carried out. Something in the agreements did bind the monitoring: the completion report says external monitoring of safeguard implementation was carried out "in accordance with the legal agreements", though neither document prints that term's wording. When Tongliang's village land was compensated as a lease, the report says the arrangement was "finally corrected per the Bank requirements" at loan closing, three years after the works were finished. The requirement at work there is OP 4.12 through the resettlement plans, not a covenant either document quotes.

The appraisal document of 25 May 2005 sets out three conditions of effectiveness: implementation agreements acceptable to the Bank between the Government and the three project provinces; execution of a tripartite arrangement by the United Kingdom's Department for International Development, the borrower and the Bank; and completion of that department's first deposit into the trust fund. Disbursement was then held back province by province: no money could be drawn for Guangxi, Sichuan or Yunnan until the province had trained its county project office staff in the financial management manual and the Bank's disbursement procedures, satisfactory to the Bank. The standing covenants required the borrower to keep the leading group and the provincial and county project offices staffed and resourced acceptably to the Bank, to furnish annual work plans by 31 October each year, and to carry out the project in accordance with the project implementation manual. That manual is where the land rules sat: it contained the environmental management plan, the overall resettlement policy framework, an ethnic minority planning framework with six development plans, and the participation, phasing and procurement manuals, and no part of it could be amended without the Bank's prior agreement. Two further covenants bound the money's use: at least half of cumulative spending, loan and counterpart funds together, had to fall on components 2 to 6, and farmers were not to be required to contribute to cost recovery for those components. Environmental assessment (OP 4.01), indigenous peoples (OD 4.20) and involuntary resettlement (OP 4.12) were triggered, at Environmental Category B. Land taking was expected to be limited and scattered, with no physical relocation, so the framework guided planning where land was needed, and resettlement action plans were prepared for the first year's works.
